candidates.title: asyncio: Windows socket reset during Proactor cleanup skips socket closure and transport detachment

labels.name: type-bug
labels.description: An unexpected behavior, bug, or error

labels.name: stdlib
labels.description: Standard Library Python modules in the Lib/ directory

candidates.body:
## Bug description

On Windows, `_ProactorBasePipeTransport._call_connection_lost()` can raise `ConnectionResetError: [WinError 10054]` from `self._sock.shutdown(socket.SHUT_RDWR)` while cleaning up a connection. The exception escapes into the event loop's exception handler before the subsequent socket closure, server detachment, and `_called_connection_lost = True` execute.

This was observed in an active application on CPython 3.14.5 (Windows), producing `Exception in callback _ProactorBasePipeTransport._call_connection_lost()` errors. The application continued running. The defect is the interrupted cleanup, beyond the unexpected error log: a socket can remain open until later finalization, and transport bookkeeping remains incomplete.

## Deterministic reproducer

This standard-library-only example injects the observed socket-shutdown error and calls the unmodified CPython cleanup method. It demonstrates the skipped cleanup without depending on network timing; it does not reproduce the original TCP reset timing. Run it on Windows in a fresh interpreter without an application-installed asyncio patch.

```python
from asyncio.proactor_events import _ProactorBasePipeTransport
from types import SimpleNamespace
from unittest.mock import Mock

reset = ConnectionResetError("connection reset during shutdown")
reset.winerror = 10054
sock = Mock()
sock.shutdown.side_effect = reset
server = Mock()
transport = SimpleNamespace(
    _called_connection_lost=False,
    _protocol=Mock(),
    _sock=sock,
    _server=server,
)

try:
    _ProactorBasePipeTransport._call_connection_lost(transport, None)
except ConnectionResetError:
    print("ConnectionResetError escaped cleanup")

print("socket.close calls:", sock.close.call_count)
print("server detach calls:", server._detach.call_count)
print("cleanup complete:", transport._called_connection_lost)
```

Observed output on CPython 3.14.5:

```text
ConnectionResetError escaped cleanup
socket.close calls: 0
server detach calls: 0
cleanup complete: False
```

## Expected behavior

An already-reset socket should still be closed and the transport detached and marked complete. Handle the expected reset around the socket shutdown operation, while ensuring remaining cleanup runs. Exceptions from `protocol.connection_lost()` and unexpected shutdown failures should remain observable; broadly suppressing exceptions around the whole callback would hide unrelated failures.

A potential improvement would prevent noisy error log messages by catching 'reasonable' shutdown failures and logging them via asyncio's debug logger (if debug mode is enabled for that proactor transport's event loop). Either way, shutdown errors should not cause cleanup to be skipped.

## CPython versions tested on

CPython 3.14.5, Windows x86-64. Both the application traceback and the deterministic reproducer were observed on this version.

Source inspection, rather than execution on those interpreters, found the same method implementation in releases 3.14.6–3.14.9 and 3.15.0–3.15.1. See the [3.14.5 source](https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/v3.14.5/Lib/asyncio/proactor_events.py) and [3.15.1 source](https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/v3.15.1/Lib/asyncio/proactor_events.py).

## Related reports

- The same shutdown traceback appears in [a comment on #125981](https://github.com/python/cpython/issues/125981#issuecomment-2439619729), a closed issue about `SSL: APPLICATION_DATA_AFTER_CLOSE_NOTIFY`. I could not find a dedicated issue tracking the interrupted Proactor socket cleanup.
- [#149388](https://github.com/python/cpython/issues/149388) concerned `WinError 6` from `PipeHandle.close()` in this callback. That issue was fixed in `PipeHandle`; this report concerns `WinError 10054` from the preceding socket `shutdown()` call.

<!-- gh-linked-prs -->
### Linked PRs
* gh-160600
<!-- /gh-linked-prs -->

linked_prs.title: gh-160429: Always close the socket in proactor _call_connection_lost()
linked_prs.body:
In `_ProactorBasePipeTransport._call_connection_lost()`, a `ConnectionError` from the socket shutdown call (e.g. `ConnectionResetError` / WinError 10054 when the peer has already reset the connection) escaped before the socket was closed, the transport was detached from its server and `_called_connection_lost` was set.

This change:
- ignores `ConnectionError` from the shutdown call: the connection is already gone, so there is nothing left to shut down;
- runs the rest of the cleanup (close the socket, detach from the server, mark the transport as done) in a `finally` block, so any other unexpected error still propagates but no longer skips the cleanup.

Tests use a mocked socket, so they run on all platforms. Both new tests fail on `main` and pass with the fix.

Closes gh-160429.

Prepared with AI assistance, then reviewed and tested before submission.

candidates.title: `hasattr(stream, "buffer") fails with ValueError if buffer is detached

labels.name: type-bug
labels.description: An unexpected behavior, bug, or error

labels.name: extension-modules
labels.description: C modules in the Modules dir

candidates.body:
### Bug report

```python
>>> stream  =  open("example.txt", "w")
>>> hasattr(stream, "buffer")
True
>>> stream.detach()
<_io.BufferedWriter name='example.txt'>
>>> hasattr(stream, "buffer")
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<python-input-2>", line 1, in <module>
    hasattr(stream, "buffer")
    ~~~~~~~^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
ValueError: underlying buffer has been detached
```

This occurs with Python 3.14.9 and 3.15.1, but not with earlier versions such as 3.14.8 and 3.15.0. Tested both on Linux and on Windows. I consider `hasattr` failing with an exception pretty bad, especially when using it with standard library objects, and the behavior changing in a bug fix release makes it even worse.

I noticed this when a unit test for our custom `isatty` utility started to fail (https://github.com/robotframework/robotframework/issues/5825). We have that utility so that we can safely check is a stream connected to console or not. It used to look like this:

```python
def isatty(stream):
    # first check if buffer was detached
    if hasattr(stream, "buffer") and stream.buffer is None:
        return False
    if not hasattr(stream, "isatty"):
        return False
    try:
        return stream.isatty()
    except ValueError:  # Occurs if file is closed.
        return False
```

I already fixed this in our end by simply removing the separate detached buffer check. `stream.isatty()` raised a ValueError if its buffer is detached, similarly when the stream is closed, and we already handle that. Apparently the separate check was added before handling closed streams and nobody noticed earlier that the check is redundant.

### CPython versions tested on:

3.14, 3.15

### Operating systems tested on:

Linux, Windows

<!-- gh-linked-prs -->
### Linked PRs
* gh-160467
<!-- /gh-linked-prs -->

linked_prs.title: gh-160427: Return None from TextIOWrapper.buffer once detached
linked_prs.body:
Fixes gh-160427.

`TextIOWrapper.buffer` raises `ValueError: underlying buffer has been detached`
once the wrapper is detached, so `hasattr(stream, "buffer")` raises instead of
returning a boolean. This is a regression in 3.14.9 and 3.15.1, introduced by
gh-157364.

That change replaced the `buffer` member descriptor with a getter that calls
`buffer_access_safe()`, which raises whenever `self->buffer` is NULL. Before
gh-157364 the attribute was exposed as
`{"buffer", _Py_T_OBJECT, offsetof(textio, buffer), Py_READONLY}`, and a NULL
object member reads as `None`. `_pyio.TextIOWrapper.buffer` still returns
`self._buffer`, which is `None` after detach, so the two implementations now
disagree.

The fix returns `None` from the getter when the wrapper is detached but
initialised. `buffer_access_safe()` is untouched, so every other caller keeps
the existing protection, and the uninitialised case still raises.

One existing test needed updating: `test_reentrant_detach_during_read` asserted
the `ValueError` from `wrapper.buffer`. Its subject is that the buffer survives
the read and the wrapper does not crash, which still holds, so it now asserts
`wrapper.buffer is None`.

Tests: `./python -m test test_io` passes, 1,066 tests. `test_detach` now also
asserts the attribute is `None` and that `hasattr` works after detach.

I used an AI assistant to help trace the regression and prepare the patch, and
I have reviewed every line of it.

candidates.title: The punycode incremental encoder and decoder transform each chunk separately

labels.name: type-bug
labels.description: An unexpected behavior, bug, or error

labels.name: stdlib
labels.description: Standard Library Python modules in the Lib/ directory

candidates.body:
## Bug description

`encodings.punycode` registers an `IncrementalEncoder` and `IncrementalDecoder`, but they just run the whole-string transform on every chunk they are given, so anything fed in more than one piece comes out wrong:

```python
>>> import codecs
>>> 'ab'.encode('punycode')
b'ab-'
>>> encoder = codecs.getincrementalencoder('punycode')()
>>> encoder.encode('a') + encoder.encode('b', final=True)
b'a-b-'
>>> b'a-b-'.decode('punycode')
'a-b'
```

Punycode encodes the positions of the non-ASCII characters relative to the whole label, so a chunk cannot be encoded without the rest of the string; the same goes for decoding. The classes are two lines each, [`Lib/encodings/punycode.py` lines 226-234](https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/6e1bd24e4d88a5b691779ae74e09fa044140891f/Lib/encodings/punycode.py#L226-L234), and ignore `final` altogether. This is half known: `test_codecs.py` lists `punycode` in `broken_unicode_with_stateful` ("encodings that don't work in stateful mode") and skips the chunked part of `test_basics` for it, but nothing says so in the docs, and the classes are still registered and handed out by `codecs.getincrementalencoder()`, `codecs.iterencode()` and `StreamWriter`.

I think the right fix is to buffer until `final` (the `BufferedIncrementalEncoder` and `BufferedIncrementalDecoder` base classes make that a few lines: `_buffer_encode` returns `(b'', 0)` until `final`), since that keeps `codecs.iterencode`, `StreamWriter` and friends working for anyone who hands them the whole label at once, which is presumably every current user. The `idna` codec already does something like it, buffering up to each `.`.

Related: #64331 (many incremental codecs do not handle fragmented data) mentions punycode in passing, in a list taken from that same `test_codecs.py` entry, but does not go into it.

Found by the Hypothesis tests in [#160155](https://github.com/python/cpython/pull/160155), where it is pinned as `PunycodeIncrementalBug.test_chunked_encode` under `expectedFailure`; the chunked tests there leave `punycode` out otherwise.

## CPython versions tested on

CPython main (6e1bd24e4d8)

## Operating systems tested on

Linux

<!-- gh-linked-prs -->
### Linked PRs
* gh-160599
<!-- /gh-linked-prs -->

linked_prs.title: gh-160308: Buffer input in the punycode incremental codec until final
linked_prs.body:
The punycode `IncrementalEncoder` and `IncrementalDecoder` ran the whole-string transform on each chunk and ignored `final`, so chunked input produced wrong output (e.g. `b'a-b-'` instead of `b'ab-'`). Punycode encodes the positions of non-ASCII characters relative to the whole string, so a chunk cannot be transformed on its own.

They now derive from `BufferedIncrementalEncoder` / `BufferedIncrementalDecoder` and buffer the input until `final` is true, as suggested in the issue. `codecs.iterencode()`/`iterdecode()` now give correct results, and `getstate()`/`setstate()`/`reset()` work through the buffered base classes.

Behaviour note: a caller that uses the incremental classes directly with a whole label but never passes `final=True` now gets empty output, since nothing is emitted until the input is known to be complete. That is the documented contract of incremental codecs, but it is a visible change for such code.

`punycode` stays in `broken_unicode_with_stateful` in `test_codecs`, because the `StreamReader`/`StreamWriter` classes still use the stateless codec per chunk; this PR only fixes the incremental classes.

Closes gh-160308.

candidates.title: symtable: a name read only inside an inlined comprehension is not marked as referenced (3.12+)

labels.name: type-bug
labels.description: An unexpected behavior, bug, or error

candidates.body:
# Bug report

### Bug description

Since PEP 709 (3.12), `symtable` no longer creates a child table for a list, set or dict comprehension. The 3.12
What's New says the comprehension's locals now appear in the enclosing function's table (gh-109292).

However, a name from the **enclosing** scope that is read *only* inside the inlined comprehension is no longer marked
as referenced in the enclosing function's table, and no child table records the read either. The read becomes
invisible to `symtable` users. On 3.9 (and, as far as I know, up to 3.11), the read appears in the comprehension's own
`listcomp` table. Generator expressions, which are still separate scopes, are unaffected.

Reproduction:

```python
"""Minimal reproduction: since PEP 709 (Python 3.12), a name read only inside an inlined list comprehension is not
marked as referenced in the enclosing function's symbol table, and no child table holds it either.
Run with several interpreters: python3.9 shows the read (in a 'listcomp' child table); 3.12 and 3.14 lose it."""
import symtable, sys

SRC = '''
def f(xs, k):
    return [x + k for x in xs]      # list comprehension: inlined since 3.12

def g(xs, k):
    return list(x + k for x in xs)  # generator expression: still its own scope
'''

def report():
    top = symtable.symtable(SRC, "<repro>", "exec")
    for fn in top.get_children():
        if fn.get_name() not in ("f", "g"):
            continue                 # skip implicit scopes such as __annotate__ (3.14)
        k = fn.lookup("k")
        children = {c.get_name(): sorted(s.get_name() for s in c.get_symbols() if s.is_referenced())
                    for c in fn.get_children()}
        print(f"{sys.version.split()[0]}  {fn.get_name()}: k.is_referenced() = {k.is_referenced()};  "
              f"child tables (referenced names) = {children}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    report()
```

Output (macOS; CPython 3.9.6, 3.12.12, 3.14.7):

```
3.9.6  f: k.is_referenced() = False;  child tables (referenced names) = {'listcomp': ['k', 'x']}
3.9.6  g: k.is_referenced() = False;  child tables (referenced names) = {'genexpr': ['k', 'x']}
3.12.12  f: k.is_referenced() = False;  child tables (referenced names) = {}
3.12.12  g: k.is_referenced() = False;  child tables (referenced names) = {'genexpr': ['k', 'x']}
3.14.7  f: k.is_referenced() = False;  child tables (referenced names) = {}
3.14.7  g: k.is_referenced() = False;  child tables (referenced names) = {'genexpr': ['k', 'x']}
```

**Expected:** in `f`, `k.is_referenced()` should be `True`, since `k` is read in `f`'s body now that the comprehension
is part of `f`'s scope. Alternatively, `symtable` should expose the inlined comprehension's references some other way.

**Impact:** tools that use `symtable` to find unused parameters or variables, or dead code, get false "unused"
results. In a scan of 35,562 function scopes, this caused 1,885 false disagreements against the compiled bytecode.

**Related:** gh-109292 (the documentation of the PEP 709 change to symtable); gh-124697 (refactoring of inlined
comprehensions), which may already fix this on main. I have not tested 3.15 / main.

### CPython versions tested on:

3.12, 3.14

### Operating systems tested on:

macOS

* gh-160457
<!-- /gh-linked-prs -->

candidates.body:
### Feature or enhancement

CPython's `_curses` module does not expose the complete core curses API.
Several bindings are missing or incomplete compared with the underlying
ncurses interface.

The missing functionality includes terminal and termcap operations,
video operations, soft-label operations, `mcprint()`, and
`ripoffline()`. Some related curses functionality is already present in
the current development branch but needs to be completed and integrated
consistently with the current stateful module architecture.

This issue intentionally concerns the core curses API only. The curses
form and menu APIs are separate and are not part of this issue.

## Proposed solution

Port the remaining core curses bindings using the current CPython
module-state and Argument Clinic conventions, and add the corresponding
tests and documentation.

## Summary

Complete the core curses bindings in CPython and adapt the port to the
current stateful curses module architecture.

The change covers the broader curses core API, including:

- window and screen lifecycle operations
- input and output operations
- character and string handling
- colors, attributes, and wide-character support
- terminal and termcap functionality
- soft-label and video operations
- `ripoffline`
- associated tests and documentation

Existing functionality already present on `main` is preserved and
integrated with the port. The curses form and menu APIs are intentionally
excluded from this change.

## Tests

- `make -j2`
- `TERM=dumb ./python -m test -u curses test_curses -v`

Result:

- 192 tests passed
- 45 tests skipped
- The skipped tests depend on ncurses 6.5; the development container
  provides ncurses 6.4.

## Notes

The implementation uses the current CPython module-state and Argument
Clinic conventions rather than copying the older implementation
verbatim.

Closes gh-160141

candidates.body:
# Feature or enhancement

`zipfile.Path` is developed primarily as [zipp](https://pypi.org/project/zipp)
and synced downstream into the stdlib, per the [development
methodology](https://github.com/python/importlib_metadata/wiki/Development-Methodology).
It was last synced from zipp 3.23 in gh-135276. This issue tracks the refresh
to zipp 4.1.2.

Three behavior changes are in scope:

- **`Path.iterdir()` raises `NotADirectoryError`** instead of `ValueError` when
  the path is not a directory (jaraco/zipp#154, released in zipp 4.1.0). This is
  a breaking change — `NotADirectoryError` is an `OSError`, not a `ValueError`,
  so callers catching `ValueError` are affected. Main only; no backport.
- **`glob()` and `rglob()` character classes follow shell semantics**
  (jaraco/zipp#162, released in zipp 4.1.1): a leading `!` negates, `^` is a
  literal, and neither matches a path separator. Previously the character set
  was passed through to the regex engine unchanged, so `[!a]` and `[^a]` were
  both treated as regex negation and could match separators.
- **The workaround for the `stacklevel` bug in PyPy < 7.3.19 is removed**
  (jaraco/zipp#149, released in zipp 4.0.0).

The remaining changes are test and lint cleanups that keep the two trees
byte-identical.

The `str()` fix also included in zipp 3.23.1 is being handled separately as a
backportable bugfix in gh-100609, and this refresh will build on it.

candidates.title: `ThreadPoolExecutor` tasks see the context of whichever `submit()` call started their worker thread

labels.name: type-bug
labels.description: An unexpected behavior, bug, or error

labels.name: stdlib
labels.description: Standard Library Python modules in the Lib/ directory

candidates.body:
### Bug report

### Bug description:

When `sys.flags.thread_inherit_context` is true (the default on the free-threaded build), `ThreadPoolExecutor` workers copy the context of the `submit()` call that happened to start them, and every later task on that worker sees that copy:

```python
import contextlib
import contextvars
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor

precision = contextvars.ContextVar("precision", default=8)


@contextlib.contextmanager
def printoptions(p):
    token = precision.set(p)
    try:
        yield
    finally:
        precision.reset(token)


def fmt(x):
    return f"{x:.{precision.get()}f}"


pool = ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=1)

with printoptions(2):
    print("with precision=2: ", fmt(3.14159), pool.submit(fmt, 3.14159).result())

print("no with block:     ", fmt(3.14159), pool.submit(fmt, 3.14159).result())

with printoptions(5):
    print("with precision=5: ", fmt(3.14159), pool.submit(fmt, 3.14159).result())
```

On 3.15.0t:

```
with precision=2:  3.14 3.14
no with block:      3.14159000 3.14
with precision=5:  3.14159 3.14
```

The pool column is stuck at `precision=2` because its only worker was started inside the first `with` block. With more than one worker, the value a task sees depends on which worker runs it.

[`sentry-sdk`](https://github.com/getsentry/sentry-python/blob/641517af508e55be96fa4f167a46a19844577e2a/sentry_sdk/integrations/threading.py#L143-L181), [`opentelemetry-instrumentation-threading`](https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-python-contrib/blob/de43f819a4a919213d246a23e62a1b256aeca7b9/instrumentation/opentelemetry-instrumentation-threading/src/opentelemetry/instrumentation/threading/__init__.py#L149-L171), and [`dask`](https://github.com/dask/dask/blob/6ce3740fa79bfa051ecc74c3641f8c6a46dfdc30/dask/threaded.py#L39-L59) all patch or subclass `ThreadPoolExecutor` to get this behavior.

See also https://discuss.python.org/t/enabling-thread-inherit-context-and-context-aware-warnings-by-default-on-both-builds/108205 and gh-154562.

### CPython versions tested on:

3.14, 3.15, CPython main branch

### Operating systems tested on:

macOS

* gh-160024
<!-- /gh-linked-prs -->

linked_prs.title: gh-159964: Propagate contextvars to ThreadPoolExecutor tasks
linked_prs.body:
Fixes gh-159964.

Capture a copy of the submitting thread's context for each submitted task and execute the callable within that context. This prevents a task from inheriting stale context from whichever worker happened to start first and keeps context-variable rebinding in one task isolated from subsequent tasks.

The change includes a regression test for context propagation across reused workers, documentation, and a NEWS entry.

Validation: lint and the C API documentation check pass. The full CI matrix is running; the local CPython test suite could not be run in this environment.

candidates.title: _testcapi._tuple_resize() leaks item references on allocation failure

labels.name: type-bug
labels.description: An unexpected behavior, bug, or error
new features, bugs and security fixes

candidates.body:
### Bug report

`_PyTuple_Resize()` leaks references to the tuple's elements when the underlying `PyObject_GC_Resize()` fails. It sets the caller's pointer to NULL and frees the old tuple storage with `PyObject_GC_Del()`, but does not release the references held in that storage.

The old allocation remains valid after the failed resize, so its remaining elements must be decref'ed before it is freed. For a shrinking resize, the removed tail entries have already been cleared; the retained entries still need cleanup if resizing fails.

### Reproducer

Run this with a build that includes `_testcapi`. The helper creates a private copy of the input tuple, satisfying `_PyTuple_Resize()`'s ownership requirement. The requested size exceeds the GC allocator's checked size limit because of header overhead; this does not depend on exhausting available RAM.

```python
import gc
import struct
import sys
import weakref
import _testcapi

class Item:
    pass

item = Item()
original = (item,)
ref = weakref.ref(item)

try:
    # The helper creates a private copy of the tuple before resizing it.
    # Header overhead makes this exceed the GC allocator's size limit.
    _testcapi._tuple_resize(original, sys.maxsize // struct.calcsize("P"))
except MemoryError:
    pass
else:
    raise AssertionError("expected MemoryError")

del original, item
gc.collect()
print("element released:", ref() is None)
assert ref() is None
```

Expected: `element released: True`.
Actual: `element released: False`, followed by `AssertionError`.

### CPython versions tested on

Reproduced with the unmodified runtime from CPython `main` at `21a36aa79ca0b2af49995fa1b9216b01ef98f195` (3.16.0a1+dev), with `--with-pydebug`. Only the new regression test was added; no runtime code was changed for the failing run.

Source inspection also confirms the same cleanup path in release tags [v3.14.8](https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/v3.14.8/Objects/tupleobject.c#L1004-L1011) and [v3.15.0](https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/v3.15.0/Objects/tupleobject.c#L1084-L1091). Those versions were not executed for this report.

### Operating systems tested on

macOS 27.0.1, Apple Silicon.

### Related reports

I searched for an existing report. #155053 concerns a caller dereferencing NULL after resize failure; its proposed fix does not address these leaked element references.

The bug was manually spotted and investigated, but AI tools assisted with the investigation, reproducer, and proposed fix. The reproducer and regression test were executed locally before submission.


<!-- gh-linked-prs -->
### Linked PRs
* gh-159526
<!-- /gh-linked-prs -->

linked_prs.title: gh-159514: Fix tuple item reference leak on resize allocation failure
linked_prs.body:
`_PyTuple_Resize()` frees the tuple storage after a failed `PyObject_GC_Resize()` without releasing its item references. Release the remaining items before freeing the storage. `Py_XDECREF()` also handles entries already cleared during shrinking.

Add a regression test that forces `MemoryError` through the allocator's checked size limit and verifies that the item is released. It fails before the fix and passes afterwards.

The leak was also reproduced by calling `_PyTuple_Resize()` directly through `ctypes.pythonapi`, without `_testcapi`: the caller's pointer became `NULL`, but the item remained alive. The `_testcapi` wrapper is unchanged.

Validation on Windows x64 Debug:

- `test_capi.test_tuple`, `test_capi.test_mem` and `test_tuple` pass in the standard build and the free-threaded build with the GIL disabled and enabled.
- `test_capi.test_tuple` passes `-R 3:3` in both builds.
- Allocation-failure checks cover growing, shrinking and `NULL` entries.
- `patchcheck` and `git diff --check` pass.

### Bug report

The default `mimetypes.knownfiles` are user-writeable on Windows. Instead of loading from these files the default behavior should be to only load from the registry.

See: https://www.cve.org/CVERecord?id=CVE-2024-3220)

On Windows, Currently users are being recommended to call `mimetypes.init([])` on Windows to mitigate the vulnerability.

linked_prs.title: gh-159428: Don't read mimetypes.knownfiles by default on Windows
linked_prs.body:
Make knownfiles empty on Windows so that only the registry is used by default. Files passed to init() or assigned to knownfiles explicitly are still read.

The default knownfiles are POSIX paths such as /etc/mime.types. On Windows these resolve against the root of the current drive (e.g. C:\etc\mime.types), a location that unprivileged users can usually create.

candidates.title: SystemExit in asyncio task raises noisy warnings

labels.name: type-bug
labels.description: An unexpected behavior, bug, or error

labels.name: stdlib
labels.description: Standard Library Python modules in the Lib/ directory

candidates.body:
### Bug report

This might be related to #102572 and/or #108549, but I think it's a distinct issue.

```python
import asyncio
import sys

async def task():
    try:
        sys.exit(2)
    except BaseException as e:
        print(f"task() saw exception: {e!r}")
        # print(traceback.format_exc())
        raise

async def main():
    try:
        t = asyncio.create_task(task())
        await asyncio.sleep(2)
        await t
    except BaseException as e:
        print(f"main() saw exception: {e!r}")
        # print(traceback.format_exc())
        raise

try:
    asyncio.run(main())
except BaseException as e:
    print(f"top level saw exception: {e!r}")
    # print(traceback.format_exc())
    raise
```

This prints:

```
task() saw exception: SystemExit(2)
main() saw exception: CancelledError()
top level saw exception: SystemExit(2)
Task exception was never retrieved
future: <Task finished name='Task-2' coro=<task() done, defined at /home/marcan/tmp/asynctest.py:4> exception=SystemExit(2)>
[ snip traceback ]
```

It seems when the subtask raises `SystemExit`, the scheduler cancels all other tasks (including the main task), then re-raises the `SystemExit` to the top level. However, since `main()` was cancelled, the subtask is never awaited. This then prints an arguably spurious warning.

In this case, the exception *was* effectively retrieved: it cancelled main and even bubbled up outside the scheduler. I think the special-case handling of `SystemExit` here should also silence the task exception retrieval warning.

If you remove the `sleep`, the warning does not occur, despite the fact that `main()` *still* gets the CancelledError (it is not seeing the `SystemExit` exception itself). So in this case, the "intent" by `main()` to retrieve the exception is sufficient to silence the warning, despite the fact that the exception wasn't *actually* propagated there.

Uncommenting the `print(traceback.format_exc())` lines shows asyncio internals "leaking" into the tracebacks, but only in the case with `sleep`.

linked_prs.title: gh-159401: Suppress duplicate task warnings for reraised BaseExceptions
linked_prs.body:
## Summary

Fixes gh-159401.

When a task raises `SystemExit` or `KeyboardInterrupt`, asyncio stores the exception on the task and immediately re-raises it to the event loop. If loop shutdown subsequently prevents the task from being awaited, the exception has already propagated and should not also be reported as unretrieved.

Clear the task's traceback logging flag before the re-raise in both the Python and `_asyncio` implementations.

## Tests

- Added coverage for both `SystemExit` and `KeyboardInterrupt`, across the Python and C task implementations.
- `./python.exe -m test -v test_asyncio.test_tasks -m 'test_step_does_not_log_reraised_base_exceptions'`
  - 8 passed
- `./python.exe -m test -v test_asyncio.test_tasks -m 'test_step_dont_swallow_systemexit_or_keyboardinterrupt'`
  - 8 passed
- `./python.exe -m test -v test_asyncio.test_tasks -m 'test_baseexception_during_cancel'`
  - 8 passed

AI assistance was used to help prepare this contribution; the behavior and tests were reviewed and run locally.

candidates.title: Free-threaded build: `marshal` output of `compile()` of an AST depends on what was compiled before

labels.name: type-bug
labels.description: An unexpected behavior, bug, or error

candidates.body:
### Bug report

On the free-threaded build, the bytes that `marshal.dumps()` gives for code
compiled from an AST object depend on which code objects were created
earlier in the process.  Compiling the same source from a string does not
have the problem.

```python
import ast, marshal, sys

SRC = "def f(a, b):\n    return g(a=1, b=2)\n"
if 'warm' in sys.argv:
    # An unrelated module compiled earlier.
    compile(ast.parse("def other(a, b):\n    return h(a=3, b=4)\n"),
            'other.py', 'exec')
d_src = marshal.dumps(compile(SRC, 'm.py', 'exec'))
d_ast = marshal.dumps(compile(ast.parse(SRC), 'm.py', 'exec'))
print(len(d_src), len(d_ast), d_src == d_ast)
```

Free-threaded main:

```
$ ./python repro.py
230 230 True
$ ./python repro.py warm
230 237 False
```

The default build prints `230 230 True` both times.

Cause: the compiler makes `co_names` / `co_localsplusnames` the same tuple
as an equal constant (keyword names, import fromlist,
`__static_attributes__`, any tuple of identifiers).  On the free-threaded
build `intern_constants()` then replaces the constant by the equal immortal
tuple of the per-interpreter table, if there is one, but not the tuple of names.
Whether the two stay one object, and so whether marshal writes a
reference or a second copy, depends on whether an equal tuple was seen
before.

`compile()` of a source string avoids this by setting
`tstate->suppress_co_const_immortalization` (gh-118527, "to get consistent
frozen outputs between the default and free-threaded builds").  The branch
of `builtin_compile_impl()` that handles AST objects returns before that is
set.

This affects tools that compile an AST and write a `.pyc`: assertion
rewriters, `SourceLoader.source_to_code()` given an AST.  Compiling the
standard library file by file from ASTs in one process, ~9% of the files
give different bytes depending on the order of the files.

### Proposed fix

Set `suppress_co_const_immortalization` around `_PyAST_Compile()` in
`compile()` as is done for source strings.  Side effect: such code no
longer gets immortal constants, as is already the case for
`compile(str)`; it also stops tools that compile many ASTs from growing
the immortal table (10000 unique functions: +141286 memory blocks on main,
+606 with the fix).

Not covered: `exec(str)`, `Py_CompileString*()`, `PyRun_*()` and
`marshal.loads()` do not set the flag and have the same history dependence.
None of them is on a path that writes `.pyc` files.

---

Discovered using Claude while doing a deep dive on pyc compilation determinism.

### CPython versions tested on:

CPython main branch

### Operating systems tested on:

_No response_

<!-- /gh-linked-prs -->

linked_prs.title: gh-159188: Do not immortalize constants in compile() of an AST
linked_prs.body:
On the free-threaded build, the `marshal` output for code compiled from an AST depended on which code objects had been created earlier in the process: ```python SRC = "def f(a, b):\n return g(a=1, b=2)\n" # optionally first: compile(ast.parse("def other(a, b):\n return h(a=3, b=4)\n"), ...) d_src = marshal.dumps(compile(SRC, 'm.py', 'exec')) d_ast = marshal.dumps(compile(ast.parse(SRC), 'm.py', 'exec')) ``` | free-threaded main | `len(d_src)` | `len(d_ast)` | | --- | --- | --- | | nothing compiled before | 230 | 230 | | an unrelated AST compiled before | 230 | 237 | The default build gives 230 in every case, and so does the free-threaded build with this PR. ### Cause and change The compiler makes a tuple of names (`co_names`, `co_localsplusnames`) the same object as an equal constant: keyword names, a `from` list, `__static_attributes__`. On the free-threaded build, `intern_constants()` replaces each constant by the equal immortal object of a per-interpreter table, if there is one, but does not replace the tuple of names. `compile()` of a source string turns that off with `tstate->suppress_co_const_immortalization` (gh-118527). The branch that handles AST objects returned before the flag was set. ```mermaid flowchart TB subgraph before["main, free-threaded"] direction TB b0["compiler: constant ('a', 'b')
is the same tuple as co_names"] b0 -- "compile(ast)" --> b2["immortalization
not suppressed"] b0 -- "compile(str)" --> b1["immortalization
suppressed"] b2 --> b4{"equal tuple already
in the immortal table?"} b4 -- yes --> b6["constant replaced, co_names not:
two tuples, marshal writes both"] b4 -- no --> b5["still one tuple"] b1 --> b3["still one tuple
marshal: object + reference"] end subgraph after["this PR"] direction TB a0["compiler: constant ('a', 'b')
is the same tuple as co_names"] a0 -- "compile(ast)" --> a1["immortalization
suppressed"] a0 -- "compile(str)" --> a1 a1 --> a3["still one tuple
marshal: object + reference"] end ``` The change is the same increment/decrement pair around `_PyAST_Compile()` in `builtin_compile_impl()` that already surrounds `_Py_CompileString()`. ### Effects - Tools that compile an AST and write a `.pyc` (assertion rewriters, `SourceLoader.source_to_code()` given an AST) get reproducible output. Compiling the standard library from ASTs in one process, 179 of 2067 files gave different bytes depending on file order; now none do. - Code from `compile(ast)` no longer has immortal constants, as is already the case for `compile(str)`. It gets them when it is later loaded from a `.pyc`. Tools that compile many ASTs stop growing the immortal table: for 10000 distinct functions, +141286 memory blocks on main, +606 with this PR. - The GIL enabled build is not affected. ### Not covered `exec()` of a string, `Py_CompileString*()`, `PyRun_*()` and `marshal.loads()` do not set the flag and keep the same dependence on history. None of them is on a path that writes `.pyc` files. ### Tests Every `TestConstantsIdentity` case (added by gh-159193) is now also compiled from an AST. `test_constants_not_immortal` (free-threaded only) checks that a tuple constant from `compile()` of a string or an AST is not immortal even after an equal one entered the table. _Authored using Claude, reviewed by me._ * Issue: gh-159188

linked_prs.title: gh-159137: Skip redundant GC resurrection analysis
linked_prs.body:
An easy win! :) The GC currently does a second reachability check because callbacks can make objects reachable again. If no weakref callback, finalizer that could run Python code, or debug writer ran, we can reuse the first result and skip that check. The finalization scan still runs. Finished generators, coroutines, and async generators use this path because their finalizers are no-ops. Free-threaded builds also skip the extra stop-the-world pause. The measurements below use a GIL-enabled build and predate the optimization for finished generators.

**Microbenchmarks**

Here each case uses 100,000 objects or allocation iterations. Values are median CPU milliseconds from six processes per case, with seven samples after two warmups. Explicit collections exclude graph construction. 

| Workload | Before | After | Less CPU time |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Retained lists | 1.552 ms | 1.565 ms | -0.79% |
| Retained nested tuples | 2.548 ms | 2.571 ms | -0.94% |
| Unreachable list cycles | 4.276 ms | 3.867 ms | 9.55% |
| Unreachable dictionary cycles | 5.498 ms | 3.565 ms | 35.16% |
| Unreachable instance cycles | 5.984 ms | 5.271 ms | 11.92% |
| Instance cycles with a no-op `__del__` | 11.785 ms | 10.744 ms | 8.84% |
| Cyclic list allocation with automatic GC | 9.533 ms | 8.456 ms | 11.29% |
| Acyclic dictionary/list allocation with automatic GC | 10.603 ms | 8.706 ms | 17.90% |

**Macrobenchmarks**

A bunch of real programs tht hevily use GC. Sphinx 8.2.3 builds all CPython HTML documentation with one worker and fresh caches: 559 source files, 599 HTML files. Mypy 2.4.0 checks its own `mypy` and `mypyc` packages: 346 files, without incremental caches or workers. A separate mypy run uses `--no-fast-exit`, then explicitly collects its analysis graph.

Values are medians from 10 runs per executable, in baseline/candidate/candidate/baseline order. Application CPU time includes imports and command execution. GC durations come from native `gc.get_stats()` counters. Cleanup collections are separate from application time.

| Workload | Before (mean CPU time) | After (mean CPU time) |
|---|---:|---:|
| Sphinx | 78.275 s | 70.560 s |
| Sphinx, separate cleanup | 0.687 s | 0.656 s |
| Mypy | 26.059 s | 26.072 s |
| Mypy with `--no-fast-exit` | 27.043 s | 26.354 s |
| Mypy with `--no-fast-exit`, separate cleanup | 1.397 s | 1.247 s |


Related to #159137.

<!-- /gh-issue-number -->

linked_prs.title: gh-159137: `gc`: Count GC survivors in `untrack_tuples()` instead of walking the young generation again
linked_prs.body:
Inspired by #159137.

After `deduce_unreachable()`, `gc_collect_main()` walks the surviving young generation twice.

`untrack_tuples()` visits every object:

https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/9028df36bb9e2942b19164f6708f9cf8a55c5ce9/Python/gc.c#L664-L676

and then `gc_list_size(young)` walks the same list again only to update `long_lived_pending` or `long_lived_total`:

https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/9028df36bb9e2942b19164f6708f9cf8a55c5ce9/Python/gc.c#L1517-L1535

So the idea is to `untrack_tuples()` to return the number of objects that stay tracked, and use it instead of `gc_list_size(young)`.

### Microbenchmark

Full collections on a heap that stays alive for the whole run. macOS 27 (M4 Air), release build w/o PGO. Median of 6 processes per binary, interleaved A/B/B/A:

| heap | `main` (`9028df3`) | `9028df3` + patch | |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 2M objects, dict + list + tuple per entry | 77.0 ms | 67.4 ms | -12% |
| 2M dicts with atomic values | 66.9 ms | 59.0 ms | -12% |
| 5M objects, dict + list + tuple per entry | 201.7 ms | 169.6 ms | -16% |
| 2M tuples of ints | 11.6 ms | 11.6 ms | 0% |

Unfortunately, I don't have access to Linux baremetal at the moment.

### Macrobenchmark

Sphinx 8.2.3 building the CPython HTML docs with one worker and fresh doctrees (`sphinx-build -b html -j 1 -E`), same machine and builds, 6 runs per binary interleaved A/B/B/A. GC time is the sum of `duration` from `gc.get_stats()` 

| | `main` (`9028df3`) | `9028df3` + patch | |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| CPU time | 46.00 s | 44.37 s | -3.5% |
| GC time | 10.07 s | 8.63 s | -14% |
| GC time, full collections only | 8.66 s | 7.26 s | -16% |
| CPU time outside GC | 35.93 s | 35.74 s | -0.5% |

<details>
<summary>Microbenchmark</summary>

```python
import gc, sys, time
N = int(sys.argv[1]); kind = sys.argv[2]
gc.disable()
if kind == "mixed":
    keep = [({"a": i, "b": None}, [i, i], (i, i + 1)) for i in range(N // 3)]
elif kind == "tuples":
    keep = [(i, i + 1, i + 2) for i in range(N)]
elif kind == "dicts":
    keep = [{"a": i, "b": "x"} for i in range(N)]
for _ in range(2):
    gc.collect()
ts = []
for _ in range(7):
    t0 = time.perf_counter_ns(); gc.collect(); ts.append(time.perf_counter_ns() - t0)
ts.sort(); print(ts[3] / 1e6)
```

</details>

linked_prs.title: gh-159137: Keep surviving objects in order in the garbage collector
linked_prs.body:
`move_unreachable()` moves objects with zero `gc_refs` out of the generation and appends them back when they turn out to be reachable. That leaves the survivors in the order the collector reached them, so every later walk of the generation misses the cache at each step. This flags those objects in place and traverses the reachable ones from a small stack, so the generation keeps its allocation order.

**Benchmarks**

GC time from `gc.get_stats()`. Medians of four runs per executable (nine for the AST heap), in baseline/candidate/candidate/baseline order.

| Workload | GC before | GC after | Less GC time |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Sphinx building the CPython docs | 28.902 s | 21.684 s | 25.0% |
| Pylint on five stdlib packages | 2.516 s | 1.979 s | 21.3% |
| Parso parsing the standard library | 1.674 s | 0.657 s | 60.8% |
| sqlglot parsing and transpiling 4,000 queries | 4.762 s | 3.690 s | 22.5% |
| Beautiful Soup parsing 90 HTML pages | 2.443 s | 1.764 s | 27.8% |
| Black checking three stdlib packages | 1.098 s | 1.019 s | 7.3% |
| Full collection of 720,000 live AST objects | 292.4 ms | 113.0 ms | 61.3% |
| **Geometric mean** | | | **35.5%** |

Collector cycles on the Pylint run. Width is the share before the change, blue frames take fewer cycles after it:

![pylint](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/pablogsal/cpython/8ad99f673a9e217a61e100587c98353d95ed3db3/diff-pylint-pr159152.png)

linked_prs.title: gh-159137: Untrack tuples and count survivors in move_unreachable()
linked_prs.body:
After finding the surviving objects, the collector walks them two more times: once in `untrack_tuples()` and once in `gc_list_size()` just to count them. `move_unreachable()` already visits each survivor, so this does both there and drops the two walks.

**Benchmarks**

GC time from `gc.get_stats()`. Medians of four runs per executable (nine for the AST heap), in baseline/candidate/candidate/baseline order.

| Workload | GC before | GC after | Less GC time |
|---|---:|---:|---:|

linked_prs.title: gh-159137: Restore known-root marking for the GIL garbage collector
linked_prs.body:
Part of gh-159137.

This brings back known-root marking for full collections in the GIL build. This was added it to the incremental collector in #127110, and it was removed when #148746 restored the generational collector. Excluding objects already known to be alive from trial reference counting is still useful without incremental collection. The free-threaded mark-alive pass in #128808 uses the same underlying idea.

linked_prs.title: gh-159137: Copy and subtract the GC reference counts in one walk
linked_prs.body:
The collector walks the generation once in `update_refs()` to copy every reference count into the GC header, and again in `subtract_refs()` to subtract the references between the collected objects. In a full collection every tracked object is in the list, so the second walk needs nothing from the first, and this does both in one walk. An object that is decremented before the walk reaches it still holds its `_gc_prev` pointer, and the walk recovers the decrements from the difference with the pointer it knows was there.

**Benchmarks**

CPU time spent in the collector, taken in `gc.callbacks`. Six runs per executable in baseline/candidate/candidate/baseline order; medians of the runs taken while the machine was quiet.

| Workload | GC before | GC after | Less GC time |

candidates.title: 3.13.16: test_math fails to import on musl (linked_to_musl() returns bool, compared to tuple)

labels.name: type-bug
labels.description: An unexpected behavior, bug, or error

candidates.body:
# Bug report

### Bug description:

The 3.13 backport of gh-152563 (#155753, commit 8e85d73bd6) changed the skip condition of `FMATests.test_fma_zero_result` in `Lib/test/test_math.py` to:

```python
or (support.linked_to_musl() and support.linked_to_musl() < (1, 2, 6)),  # gh-131032
```

On `main`/3.14, `support.linked_to_musl()` returns the musl version as a tuple. On the 3.13 branch it still returns a plain `bool` (`return ('musl' in stdout)`), so on a musl-based system the condition evaluates `True < (1, 2, 6)` and raises:

```
TypeError: '<' not supported between instances of 'bool' and 'tuple'
```

Because this happens inside the `@unittest.skipIf(...)` decorator, it is raised at class definition time and `test_math` fails to import entirely. `test_cmath` imports from `test.test_math`, so it fails too. On glibc the expression short-circuits on `False`, so it doesn't show up there.

This is a regression in 3.13.16. A visible consequence: building 3.13.16 on Alpine Linux with `--enable-optimizations` fails, because both modules are part of the PGO training set:

```
[ 8/43] test_cmath failed (uncaught exception)
[27/43] test_math failed (uncaught exception)
Total test files: run=43/43 failed=2
Result: FAILURE
make: *** [Makefile:911: profile-run-stamp] Error 2
```

To fix it, either restore the previous `or support.linked_to_musl(),` condition on 3.13, or also backport the `linked_to_musl()` change that returns a version tuple.

Seen in Home Assistant's Alpine-based Python images: https://github.com/home-assistant/docker-base/pull/402

### CPython versions tested on:

3.13

### Operating systems tested on:

Linux

linked_prs.title: [3.13] gh-159015: Fix test_math import on musl
linked_prs.body:
The 3.13 backport of gh-152563 (#155753) changed the skip condition of `test_fma_zero_result` to `support.linked_to_musl() < (1, 2, 6)`. That works on `main`/3.14, where `linked_to_musl()` returns the musl version tuple (gh-90548). On 3.13 it still returns a `bool`, so on musl the condition raises `TypeError` while the class is being defined. `test_math` then fails to import, and `test_cmath` (which imports from it) fails too. This breaks `--enable-optimizations` builds of 3.13.16 on Alpine.

This PR restores the previous condition, so the test is skipped on musl again, as it was before 3.13.16. It's a 3.13-only fix; `main` and 3.14 are not affected.

candidates.title: Windows: `import hashlib` loads user32.dll and the GDI DLLs through libcrypto; delay-load user32

labels.name: extension-modules
labels.description: C modules in the Modules dir

labels.name: pending
labels.description: The issue will be closed if no feedback is provided

candidates.body:
### Description

On Windows, importing `hashlib` maps `user32.dll`, `gdi32.dll`, `gdi32full.dll`, `win32u.dll` and
`imm32.dll` into the process. So do `hmac`, `secrets`, `ssl`, `asyncio`, `urllib.request`,
`http.client`, and therefore pip and most network code. CPython does not use any of them.

They come from `libcrypto-3.dll`, which `_hashlib` and `_ssl` link. Its import table names three
user32 functions:

- `GetProcessWindowStation` and `GetUserObjectInformationW`, called by `OPENSSL_isservice()`;
- `MessageBoxW`, called by `OPENSSL_showfatal()`.

In OpenSSL 3.0 to 3.5, both are reached only from `OPENSSL_die()`, the internal-error abort
path (`crypto/cryptlib.c`). The CAPI engine's certificate dialog also calls `OPENSSL_isservice()`,
but CPython does not load that engine. The import is still resolved when `_hashlib.pyd` loads,
and with it user32's own dependencies.

gh-155435 fixed the same thing for `_ctypes` (ole32), noting that a plain `python.exe` no longer
loads user32. gh-89883 removed shlwapi for the same kind of start-up cost. `_hashlib` and `_ssl`
still pull user32 in, through OpenSSL.

```
python -c "import hashlib", then tasklist /m for that process:
python.org 3.14.8    (OpenSSL 3.5.9)   pass: 14 DLLs   import hashlib: 24 DLLs, incl. user32 gdi32 gdi32full win32u imm32
python.org 3.15.0rc3 (OpenSSL 3.5.9)   pass: 14 DLLs   import hashlib: 25 DLLs, the same five
```

### Proposed change

Link libcrypto with user32 delay-loaded, so the three functions are bound on first call, i.e. only
on the abort path. One line in `PCbuild/openssl.vcxproj`, which `PCbuild/prepare_ssl.bat` uses to
build the OpenSSL binaries:

```diff
-$(Perl) "$(opensslDir)\configure" $(OpenSSLPlatform) no-asm no-uplink
+$(Perl) "$(opensslDir)\configure" $(OpenSSLPlatform) no-asm no-uplink "LDFLAGS=/nologo /debug /DELAYLOAD:user32.dll" LDLIBS=delayimp.lib
```

- `LDFLAGS` replaces the VC targets' default, which is `/nologo /debug` in both 3.0 and 3.5.
- `LDLIBS` adds the delay-load helper. Configure still links the target's own `ex_libs`
  (ws2_32, gdi32, advapi32, crypt32, user32).
- `libssl` imports nothing from user32. It gets a harmless LNK4199 ("/DELAYLOAD:user32.dll
  ignored").

It takes effect with the next rebuild of the cpython-bin-deps OpenSSL binaries; nothing else in
the tree changes.

### Measurements

**Build.** OpenSSL 3.5.9 (main's pin), x64, built with main's `openssl.vcxproj` as
`prepare_ssl.bat` runs it, once as is and once with the change.

**Setup.** Three copies of the python.org 3.15.0rc3 embeddable distribution (OpenSSL 3.5.9),
differing only in `libcrypto-3.dll` and `libssl-3.dll`:
- `python.org`: as shipped;
- `rebuilt`: main's project as is; the control;
- `delay-load`: with the change.

**Method.** One machine (i9-14900K, Windows 11). 20 interleaved passes, a fresh process per
measurement. Medians, and the paired difference `delay-load − rebuilt` with a bootstrap 95% CI.

| | python.org | rebuilt | delay-load | delay-load − rebuilt |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `import _hashlib`, in-process | 4.94 ms | 4.94 ms | 2.92 ms | **−1.99 ms [−2.14, −1.95]**, 20/20 passes |
| `python -c "import hashlib"`, start to exit | 27.0 ms | 26.8 ms | 24.7 ms | **−2.3 ms [−3.0, −1.5]** |
| `LoadLibraryExW(_hashlib.pyd)` alone | 3.20 ms | 3.11 ms | 1.14 ms | −2.00 ms [−2.06, −1.90] |
| DLLs newly mapped by that load | 9 | 9 | 3 | −6 |
| `import ssl` after `_hashlib` | 8.53 ms | 8.59 ms | 8.49 ms | −0.1 [−0.3, +0.1] |
| `python -c pass` (control) | 20.9 ms | 20.9 ms | 20.7 ms | 0.0 [−0.5, +0.4] |

**Reading the table.**
- The control matches the python.org binaries within 0.2 ms on every row.
- `import ssl` does not change: the user32 cost goes to whichever of `_hashlib` and `_ssl` loads
  libcrypto first.
- The same change on a 3.14.4 PGO build with OpenSSL 3.0.19 measured −2.05 ms [−2.16, −1.95] for
  `import _hashlib`.

**Checks** on 3.15.0rc3 with the delay-load libcrypto:
- `test_hashlib test_hmac test_ssl test_httplib test_urllib2_localnet test_asyncio.test_ssl
  test_asyncio.test_sslproto` pass: 679 tests, 44 skipped.
- The exported `OPENSSL_isservice()`, called from a small console program, still works: user32 is
  absent before the call, is loaded by it, and the result is the same as with the stock DLL.

**In a real workflow.** `pip install requests==2.32.5` from sdists (build isolation, no network) starts 21 interpreters, 20 of which import `_hashlib`. Timing each first `import _hashlib` in place, the change saves 2.0 ms per process, about 40 ms per install.

### Notes

- OpenSSL could instead bind these functions with `GetProcAddress` on the abort path. That would
  help every Windows consumer, but it is a source change in a dependency. The linker flag needs
  none and is easy to drop again.
- Other distributions that build their own OpenSSL can use the same flag.

linked_prs.title: gh-159008: Delay load user32.dll in libcrypto on Windows
linked_prs.body:
`_hashlib` and `_ssl` link `libcrypto-3.dll`. Its import table names three `user32.dll` functions:

- `GetProcessWindowStation` and `GetUserObjectInformationW`, used by `OPENSSL_isservice()`;
- `MessageBoxW`, used by `OPENSSL_showfatal()`.

Both are only reached from `OPENSSL_die()`, i.e. when OpenSSL aborts on an internal error. The
import is still resolved at load time, so `import hashlib` (and `hmac`, `secrets`, `ssl`,
`asyncio`, `urllib.request`, `http.client` ...) maps `user32.dll`, `gdi32.dll`, `gdi32full.dll`,
`win32u.dll` and `imm32.dll` into the process. A plain `python.exe` does not load any of them.
Since gh-155435, `_ctypes` no longer does either.

This links libcrypto with `/DELAYLOAD:user32.dll`. The three functions are then bound on first
call, on the abort path. The change is one line in `PCbuild/openssl.vcxproj`, so it takes effect
the next time the OpenSSL binaries in cpython-bin-deps are built with `prepare_ssl.bat`.

- `LDFLAGS` replaces the VC targets' default `/nologo /debug`, which is unchanged from 3.0 to 3.5.
- `LDLIBS=delayimp.lib` adds the delay-load helper; Configure still links the target's own
  `ex_libs` (ws2_32, gdi32, advapi32, crypt32, user32).
- `libssl` gets the same flag but imports nothing from user32. It links with LNK4199, a
  "/DELAYLOAD:user32.dll ignored" warning, and no other change.

**Built with this branch's `openssl.vcxproj`**: OpenSSL 3.5.9, x64, Release; `msbuild
PCbuild\openssl.vcxproj` as `prepare_ssl.bat` runs it, once without and once with the change.

- `dumpbin /dependents`: USER32.dll moves to the delay-load table, and nothing else changes.
- The result goes into a 3.15.0rc3 embeddable distribution, which uses OpenSSL 3.5.9:
  - `import hashlib` loads no user32/GDI DLL;
  - `test_hashlib test_hmac test_ssl test_httplib test_urllib2_localnet test_asyncio.test_ssl
    test_asyncio.test_sslproto` pass: 679 tests, 44 skipped.
- `OPENSSL_isservice()` (exported), called from a small console program, still works: user32 is
  absent before the call and loaded by it, and the result (0) is the same as with the stock DLL.

only in libcrypto/libssl; 20 interleaved passes, fresh process each; medians, paired
bootstrap 95% CIs):

| | python.org | without this change | with it | difference |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `import _hashlib`, in-process | 4.94 ms | 4.94 ms | 2.92 ms | **−1.99 ms [−2.14, −1.95]** (20/20 passes) |
| `python -c "import hashlib"`, start to exit | 27.0 ms | 26.8 ms | 24.7 ms | **−2.3 ms [−3.0, −1.5]** |
| DLLs newly mapped by loading `_hashlib.pyd` | 9 | 9 | 3 | −6 |
| `import ssl` after `_hashlib` | 8.53 ms | 8.59 ms | 8.49 ms | −0.1 [−0.3, +0.1] |
| `python -c pass` (control) | 20.9 ms | 20.9 ms | 20.7 ms | 0.0 [−0.5, +0.4] |

On a 3.14.4 PGO build with OpenSSL 3.0.19, the same change measured −2.05 ms [−2.16, −1.95] for `import _hashlib`.

On CPython 3.14 with the experimental JIT, this standard-library-only command produces UBSan misaligned-access reports in `Python/jit.c`, followed by an ASan SEGV. It happens both with and without the tail-call interpreter:

```sh
./python -c 'import re; re.compile(r"[\x00-\uffff]")'
```

candidates.title: Optimize dict insertion and deletion by avoiding a second probe
candidates.body:
### Feature or enhancement

### Proposal

Inserting a str key probes the dict index table twice: the lookup decides
whether the key is present, then `find_empty_slot()` walks the same probe
sequence to find the slot to insert into.  Deleting probes twice as well
(lookup + `lookdict_index()`).

I'd like the first probe to report the slot it ends on, so the
insert/delete path can reuse it:

* on a hit: the slot that refers to the entry (what `lookdict_index()`
  returns);
* on a miss: the slot `find_empty_slot()` would return (the first dummy
  in the GIL build, the empty slot in the free-threaded build).

### Scope

Only exact str keys in all-unicode tables can use it.  That comparison
(pointer equality, cached hash, `memcmp`) cannot execute Python code, therefore
the dict cannot be resized or mutated while the probe is running.  For
other keys `__eq__` can run arbitrary code and invalidate the slot, so
they keep today's two-probe behaviour.  Readers pass a NULL slot and
generate the same code as before.

### Numbers

Prototype, `Objects/dictobject.c` only.  Per-metric subprocesses, medians
of 11 runs. the dict code built with `-O3 -DNDEBUG`, otherwise a
free-threaded debug build.

| operation | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `del d[k]`, str | 47.7 ns | 41.4 ns (−13%) |
| `del d[k]`, str, many dummies | 48.6 ns | 43.0 ns (−12%) |
| `d.pop(k)`, str | 65.0 ns | 59.9 ns (−7.7%) |
| `dict.fromkeys`, str | 42.5 ns | 38.1 ns (−10%) |
| dict comprehension, str | 66.5 ns | 60.9 ns (−8.4%) |
| `d[k] = v`, existing str key | 60.0 ns | 54.2 ns (−9.6%) |
| `k in d`, str (control) | 43.6 ns | 44.4 ns (+1.9%) |
| `del` / `pop` / `d[k] = v`, int | 36.1 / 52.4 / 46.5 | 36.3 / 53.0 / 46.8 (≤1.2%) |

The reader path is instruction-for-instruction identical to main at `-O3`.
`test_dict`, `test_dictviews`, `test_dictcomps` and
`test_capi.test_watchers` pass on a free-threaded debug build.

### Status

This is @eendebakpt's `dict-insert-single-probe-v7` branch, rebased and
reshaped (thanks!).

### Has this already been discussed elsewhere?

I have already discussed this feature proposal on Discourse

### Links to previous discussion of this feature:

https://discuss.python.org/t/optimization-for-insertdict/109348

linked_prs.title: gh-158898: Optimize dict insertion and deletion by avoiding a second probe
linked_prs.body:
This is based on @eendebakpt's `dict-insert-single-probe-v7` prototype. I rebased and reshaped it on top of `main` and finished the remaining pieces. Thanks to Pieter for the prototype and for the measurements that started this.

## The problem

`do_lookup()` walks the index table's probe sequence to find a key. After that walk, the insert and delete paths walked the same sequence a second time: `find_empty_slot()` to find a slot for a new key, and `lookdict_index()` to find the slot that refers to a deleted entry. The lookup only returned the entry index, so the slot in the index table had to be recomputed.

## The change

`do_lookup()` now takes an optional `Py_ssize_t *hashpos` and reports the slot its probe ends on:

* if the key is found, the slot that refers to its entry, i.e. what `lookdict_index()` computes;
* if the key is not found, the slot where the key would be inserted: the first dummy slot in the GIL build, or the first empty slot in the free-threaded build. `do_lookup()` keeps track of the first dummy slot as `freeslot` for the GIL build.

`dict_lookup_pos()` is the writer-side entry point: it reports `hashpos` for the case described below and sets it to `-1` otherwise. `insertdict()`, `dict_setdefault_ref_lock_held()`, `_PyDict_DelItem_KnownHash_LockHeld()` and `_PyDict_Pop_KnownHash()` use it and pass `hashpos` to `insert_combined_dict()` / `delitem_common()`, which then reuse it instead of probing again. Readers pass `NULL`.

`insert_combined_dict()` invalidates `hashpos` before resizing, and debug builds assert that a reused `hashpos` matches a second probe.

Passing `NULL` on the reader paths lets the compiler eliminate the slot-tracking bookkeeping, so ordinary lookups do not pay for this optimization.

## Why only exact `str` keys

Reusing `hashpos` is only valid if the index table cannot change between the lookup and the write. This is guaranteed for exact `str` keys because the comparison cannot invoke arbitrary Python code.

For an exact `str` key in a combined all-unicode table (`DICT_KEYS_UNICODE`; the dict switches to `DICT_KEYS_GENERAL` on the first non-`str` key), the key comparison is pointer equality, cached hash comparison and `unicode_eq()` (a raw string-data comparison). None of that can run Python code, so the dict cannot be mutated, resized or cleared while the probe is running.

`PyUnicode_CheckExact` is required because subclasses may override comparison behavior and can therefore execute Python code. The table kind also guarantees that the stored keys are exact `str`.

For every other key, `compare_generic()` / `compare_unicode_generic()` call `PyObject_RichCompareBool()`, so `__eq__` can insert into, delete from, `clear()` or resize the same dict in the middle of the probe. A `hashpos` observed before that is no longer valid, so those keys keep probing again after the lookup.

Two implementation notes. The slot-reporting probe is a separate function (`unicodekeys_lookup_unicode_pos()`) and `find_empty_slot()` is not force-inlined, so `insertdict()` and `pop()` do not grow; the reader functions `unicodekeys_lookup_unicode()` and `unicodekeys_lookup_unicode_threadsafe()` generate the same code as before.

Split (shared) keys tables are handled as well: `delitem_common()` only computes `hashpos` for combined tables (deleting from a split table never touches the index table), and `insert_split_key()` reuses the slot from the lookup it already performs while holding the keys mutex.

## Affected operations

`del d[k]`, `d.pop(k)`, `d[k] = v` for absent and existing string keys, `d.setdefault(k, v)`, `dict.fromkeys()`, dict comprehensions and `d.update()` (they go through the same insert path), plus new attribute insertion through split-key dictionaries.

Lookups (`d[k]`, `k in d`, `d.get()`), iteration and resizing (`dictresize()` / `build_indices_*()`) are unchanged. `int`, mixed and otherwise generic keys keep the previous two-probe behaviour.

## Benchmarks

Method: branch vs `main` (85c03d47a24). Every metric runs in its own process, 11 alternating repetitions, median reported.

`Objects/dictobject.c` is compiled with `-O3 -DNDEBUG` and linked into an otherwise `--with-pydebug --disable-gil` build, so the dict code is optimized like a release build while the surrounding interpreter is still a debug build. This is not a PGO build.

`k in d` is included as a control whose code is identical to `main`; it measured +0.4%, which is worth keeping in mind for the smaller numbers below.

### Unicode keys (exact `str`, combined all-unicode table)

| operation | main | branch | change |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| `del d[k]` | 46.8 ns | 41.1 ns | −12.2% |
| `del d[k]`, many dummy slots | 47.7 ns | 41.7 ns | −12.5% |
| `d.pop(k)` | 62.1 ns | 58.3 ns | −6.2% |
| `d[k] = v`, existing key | 57.6 ns | 51.2 ns | −11.3% |
| `d[k] = v`, absent key | 66.3 ns | 61.3 ns | −7.4% |
| `d.setdefault(k, v)`, absent | 89.3 ns | 84.1 ns | −5.9% |
| `d.setdefault(k, v)`, present | 70.5 ns | 70.7 ns | +0.2% |
| `dict.fromkeys()` | 41.4 ns/key | 37.6 ns/key | −9.2% |
| dict comprehension | 65.8 ns/key | 59.7 ns/key | −9.3% |
| `k in d` (control, unchanged code) | 43.7 ns | 43.9 ns | +0.4% |

### int keys (GENERAL table)

| operation | main | branch | change |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| `del d[k]` | 35.4 ns | 35.4 ns | +0.1% |
| `d.pop(k)` | 51.6 ns | 52.3 ns | +1.4% |
| `d[k] = v`, existing key | 45.1 ns | 45.7 ns | +1.4% |
| `d[k] = v`, absent key | 56.4 ns | 56.1 ns | −0.6% |
| `d.setdefault(k, v)`, absent | 79.1 ns | 75.6 ns | −4.4% |
| `dict.fromkeys()` | 25.4 ns/key | 24.6 ns/key | −3.0% |
| dict comprehension | 47.8 ns | 47.3 ns | −1.1% |
| `k in d` (control) | 31.1 ns | 31.1 ns | 0.0% |

### mixed `str` + `int` keys (GENERAL table)

| operation | main | branch | change |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| `del d[k]` | 46.4 ns | 45.7 ns | −1.5% |
| `d.pop(k)` | 60.4 ns | 61.1 ns | +1.2% |
| `d[k] = v`, existing key | 62.0 ns | 64.2 ns | +3.4% |
| `d[k] = v`, absent key | 76.0 ns | 76.1 ns | +0.1% |
| `d.setdefault(k, v)`, absent | 101.5 ns | 100.8 ns | −0.7% |
| `dict.fromkeys()` | 38.2 ns/key | 37.7 ns/key | −1.5% |
| `k in d` (control) | 37.8 ns | 37.5 ns | −0.8% |

The string-key insert/delete paths are consistently faster in this build. The int and mixed paths change little overall, with individual results of a few percent in both directions; they still probe twice and only see the extra `hashpos` argument and the dispatch in `dict_lookup_pos()`.

These numbers are not enough to judge the impact on real workloads. The next step is to measure the effect on PGO builds with realistic workloads.

## Tests

* `test_dict`, `test_dictviews`, `test_dictcomps`: pass (171 tests) on a
  `--with-pydebug --disable-gil` build, with the new debug assert enabled.
* `test_capi.test_watchers`: pass (60 tests).
* A randomized differential test against `main` (str/int/mixed keys, hash
  collisions, instance attributes / split keys, deletion, `popitem()`,
  `clear()`) gives identical results.
* Compared with `main`, the generated `-O3` assembly for
  `unicodekeys_lookup_unicode()` and
  `unicodekeys_lookup_unicode_threadsafe()` is identical.

### Bug report

```python
import os

def test_env(x):
    print(f'setting X={x}')
    os.environ['X'] = x
    assert os.environ.get('X') == x, os.environ.get('X')
    os.reload_environ()
```

note also that this bug *also* results in `os.environ` diverging from the real environment (line 8 above is an assertion failure only *after* `os.reload_environ()`)

linked_prs.title: gh-158694: Slai Agent Runtime preserves empty Windows environment values
linked_prs.body:
## Summary

- Preserve empty Windows environment-variable values in the process environment and in child processes.
- Read the Windows process environment from `GetEnvironmentStringsW()` so `os.reload_environ()` also retains empty values.
- Add Windows regression coverage for `os.environ[name] = ''`, child inheritance, and `os.reload_environ()`.

Fixes gh-158694.

## Problem

On Windows, the CRT call `_wputenv(L"NAME=")` removes `NAME` from the Process Environment Block. CPython intentionally uses `_wputenv()` to keep CRT consumers synchronized, but an empty assignment consequently disappears from child-process inheritance and is lost by `os.reload_environ()`.

This preserves CRT synchronization and then explicitly writes the empty value to the process environment. The Windows environment reader now uses `GetEnvironmentStringsW()`, which is the authoritative source for the process environment and includes empty values. Hidden drive-current-directory entries remain excluded from `os.environ`.

## Validation

- Built CPython `x64 Debug` on Windows: 0 warnings, 0 errors.
- `test_os.test_os.EnvironTests.test_environ_empty_value`: passed.
- Existing `test_os.test_os.EnvironTests.test_putenv_unsetenv`: passed.
- Manual built-interpreter validation confirmed an empty value remains visible before and after `os.reload_environ()` and is inherited by a child process.
- `git diff --check`: passed.

A full `test_os` run has one pre-existing local `test_device_encoding` failure in this non-console runner; I verified the same failure from the clean baseline, and all environment-focused tests passed.

## Slai Agent Runtime context

Slai Agent Runtime encountered this while operating in a Windows automation environment that relies on child-process environment propagation. The developer authorized this contribution after the issue was reproduced and the fix was validated. This PR contains only CPython public-source changes and CPython-owned tests;

linked_prs.title: gh-158684: Remove ineffective lazy import of sysconfig from ctypes
linked_prs.body:
Fixes gh-158684.

## Root cause

`Lib/ctypes/__init__.py` declared a lazy import of `sysconfig`:

```python
lazy import sysconfig as _sysconfig
```

but the only uses of `_sysconfig` were at module scope, inside the `android` and `cygwin` branches of the `pythonapi` setup:

```python
elif _sys.platform == "android":
    pythonapi = PyDLL(_sysconfig.get_config_var("LDLIBRARY"))
elif _sys.platform == "cygwin":
    pythonapi = PyDLL(_sysconfig.get_config_var("DLLLIBRARY"))
```

Reading a lazily imported name reifies that import immediately, so the lazy import was not lazy at all on those two platforms, and on every other platform nothing ever resolved it: it just sat in `sys.lazy_modules` forever. Either way the laziness bought nothing, and retaining an unresolvable pending entry is the bug reported in gh-158684.

## Change

Drop the lazy import and do a plain conditional `import sysconfig` in the two branches that actually need it. `sysconfig` is now loaded on Android/Cygwin and is neither loaded nor retained anywhere else. Behaviour is otherwise unchanged: the same two `get_config_var()` calls produce the same `pythonapi` on the same two platforms.

## Tests

Added `test.test_lazy_import.StdlibLazyImportTests.test_ctypes_does_not_leave_sysconfig_pending`, which imports `ctypes` in a subprocess and asserts `sysconfig` is not left in `sys.lazy_modules`.

Results on 3.15.0rc3 with these files copied over its `Lib/`:

- new test against stock `ctypes`: **FAIL** - `AssertionError: ['locale', 'pkgutil', 'sysconfig', 'traceback', 'warnings']`
- new test against patched `ctypes`: **ok**
- `test.test_lazy_import`: 162 tests, **OK**
- `test.test_ctypes`: 675 tests, **OK** (40 skipped)
- `ctypes.pythonapi.Py_GetVersion()` still works

`git diff --check` is clean and the committed blobs are LF.

Note on validation scope: this machine has no MSVC toolchain (`cl.exe`), so I could not run a native CPython build or `make patchcheck`. The change is pure-Python and the suites above were run against a 3.15.0rc3 interpreter, not against a `main` build; the Android and Cygwin branches themselves could not be exercised here since this is Windows.

candidates.title: `Pool.imap(buffersize=...)` blocks all other tasks on the pool until the iterator is consumed

labels.name: type-bug
labels.description: An unexpected behavior, bug, or error

labels.name: stdlib
labels.description: Standard Library Python modules in the Lib/ directory
new features, bugs and security fixes

candidates.body:
### Bug report

### Bug description:

While an `imap()` or `imap_unordered()` iterator created with `buffersize` is waiting to be consumed, no other task submitted to the same pool is sent to the workers. If the program needs that other work before it reads more of the iterator, it deadlocks.

```python
import multiprocessing as mp

def sq(x):
    return x * x

def neg(x):
    return -x

if __name__ == '__main__':
    with mp.Pool(2) as pool:
        a = pool.imap(sq, range(10), buffersize=4)
        b = pool.imap(neg, range(10), buffersize=4)
        print(list(zip(a, b)))   # hangs forever
```

Without `buffersize`, this prints the ten pairs immediately.

A second form, with a single buffered iterator:

```python
with mp.Pool(2) as pool:
    a = pool.imap(sq, range(10), buffersize=4)
    pool.apply_async(sq, (7,)).get(timeout=5)   # raises TimeoutError
```

`ThreadPool` and `imap_unordered()` behave the same way.

**Cause:** the pool has a single task handler thread (`Pool._handle_tasks`). It iterates the generator returned by `_guarded_task_generation()`, and that generator blocks in `sema.acquire()` when the buffer is full. While it is blocked there, the thread cannot take anything else from `_taskqueue`.

Thread dump during the `zip` hang:

```text
Thread [Thread-2 (_handle_tasks)]:
  File "Lib/threading.py", line 515 in acquire
  File "Lib/multiprocessing/pool.py", line 405 in _guarded_task_generation
  File "Lib/multiprocessing/pool.py", line 551 in _handle_tasks

Main thread:
  File "Lib/multiprocessing/pool.py", line 922 in next
```

In the `zip` example, `next(b)` waits for a task that is never submitted, and the task handler waits for `a` to be read, which never happens.

**Possible directions:**

- Do not throttle inside the task handler thread. For example, submit the next item from the consumer's thread in `IMapIterator.next()`, similar to what `Executor.map(buffersize=...)` does in `concurrent.futures`.
- Or keep the current design and document that a pool should not be shared between a `buffersize` iterator and other work.

I would like to work on this. Before I write a patch, I would like to know which direction maintainers prefer.

Related: gh-158675 (results dropped after `close()`), which comes from the same blocking `sema.acquire()` in the task handler.

`buffersize` was added in gh-64192 and is new in 3.16, so no released version is affected.

CPython main branch

macOS

linked_prs.title: gh-158677: Fix Pool.imap(buffersize=...) blocking other tasks on the pool
linked_prs.body:
### Problem

With `buffersize`, `imap()` and `imap_unordered()` throttle task submission by blocking on a semaphore inside the pool's task handler thread. The pool has only one such thread, so while it waits for the iterator to be consumed, no other task on the pool is submitted. This deadlocks, for example, `zip()` over two buffered `imap()` iterators.

### Fix

The task handler no longer waits. When the buffer of an iterator is full, it sets that iterator's tasks aside and moves on to the next job. When a result is consumed, `next()` puts them back on the task queue.

The input iterable is still consumed by the task handler thread, so nothing else changes: `imap()` returns immediately and `next()` never waits for the iterable.

`close()` is unchanged: a partially consumed iterator still stops early. That is gh-158675 and is left out of this PR.

### Alternative considered

The issue suggested submitting the next task from `next()`, as `Executor.map(buffersize=...)` does. I tried that approach first but moved away from it because the iterable would then be consumed in the caller's thread. As a result, `next()` could hold a ready result while waiting for the next input item, causing a deadlock if producing that item depends on the result being handled.

### Tests

- Other tasks (`apply_async()`, a second buffered `imap()`) run while a buffered iterator is waiting to be consumed. This test fails without the fix.
- An exception raised by the iterable is propagated through `next()`. This case was not previously covered with `buffersize`.

Tested on macOS. Not tested on Linux, Windows or the free-threaded build.

No NEWS entry, since `buffersize` is new in 3.16 and not released yet.

I used Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5, effort: Medium) to help investigate the bug and develop the fix. I reviewed, understood, modified, and tested the resulting changes myself.

candidates.title: Marshal Stacksize Integer Overflow leading to Frame Crash

labels.name: type-bug
labels.description: An unexpected behavior, bug, or error

labels.name: pending
labels.description: The issue will be closed if no feedback is provided

candidates.body:
### Bug report

### Description
In `Python/marshal.c`, The `TYPE_CODE` reader accepts `stacksize` from untrusted marshal data with zero validation: `stacksize = (int)r_long(p);`

`Objects/codeobject.c:550`, When the code object is created, `co_framesize` is computed: `co->co_framesize = nlocalsplus + con->stacksize + FRAME_SPECIALS_SIZE;`

With `stacksize = INT_MAX (2147483647)` and `nlocalsplus = 3`, this overflows the signed 32-bit int and becomes `-2147483642`.

`Objects/frameobject.c:2118`, Frame allocation does the same overflow:
```c
int slots = code->co_nlocalsplus + code->co_stacksize;
PyFrameObject *f = PyObject_GC_NewVar(PyFrameObject, &PyFrame_Type, slots);
```
`Python/pystate.c:3136`, The interpreter's frame push has a bug:
```c
_PyInterpreterFrame *_PyThreadState_PushFrame(PyThreadState *tstate, size_t size) {
    assert(size < INT_MAX/sizeof(PyObject *));  // Compiled out with -DNDEBUG
    if (_PyThreadState_HasStackSpace(tstate, (int)size)) { 
        _PyInterpreterFrame *res = (_PyInterpreterFrame *)tstate->datastack_top;
        tstate->datastack_top += size;
        return res;
    }
```
- This bug only occurs when using tracing, causing discrepancy in behavior.

### PoC
```py
# main.py
import marshal, struct, types

code = compile("def f(a, b, c): return a + b + c", "<t>", "exec")
ns = {}; 
exec(code, ns)
func_code = ns['f'].__code__

# Patch stacksize to INT_MAX in the marshal stream
data = bytearray(marshal.dumps(func_code))
data[13:17] = struct.pack('<i', 0x7fffffff)  # stacksize field

# Load it: no error, valid code object
evil = marshal.loads(bytes(data))
func = types.FunctionType(evil, globals())

print("Running func without tracing...")
print(func(1, 2, 3))

import sys
sys.settrace(lambda f, e, a: None)
print("Running func with tracing...")
func(1, 2, 3)
```

#### Output
```console
Running func without tracing...
6
Running func with tracing...
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "main.py", line 22, in <module>
    func(1, 2, 3)
    ~~~~^^^^^^^^^
SystemError: Missing frame when calling trace function.
```

### CPython versions tested on:

3.15

### Operating systems tested on:

Linux
